title: Microsoft Teams: allowed list of external meeting notetaker bots
summary: The briefing accurately separates the planned allowed-bots list from the existing bot-detection policy. The roadmap facts, existing control and Teams licensing requirement are supported; searches found no documentation for the planned list's configuration or default. Minor clarifications should note the bot-registration preview's full capacity and inconsistent PowerShell examples in the external-bots guide.

claims.where: What's changing; Risk assessment: Data exposure
claims.claim: Existing Teams detection identifies external bots using signals collected during the meeting join process.
claims.quote: Teams uses built-in detection mechanisms to identify external AI bots based on signals collected during the meeting join process.

claims.claim: With bot detection enabled, detected bots are placed in the lobby irrespective of the meeting's lobby configuration.
claims.quote: The participants detected as bots are placed in the meeting lobby irrespective of the lobby configuration for the meeting.

claims.claim: The external-bots guide says organizers must explicitly admit detected bots.
claims.quote: Organizers (also presenters, depending on the meeting setting), need to explicitly admit these bots into the meeting.

claims.claim: The external-bots guide says presenters can also admit detected bots depending on the meeting setting.
claims.quote: Organizers (also presenters, depending on the meeting setting), need to explicitly admit these bots into the meeting.

claims.claim: The Bot Identification Program page instead describes detected bots as requiring organizer approval.
claims.quote: Even when a meeting allows participants to bypass the lobby, detected bots still require organizer approval before joining.

claims.claim: The existing policy defaults to When detected, require approval before joining, represented by RequireApprovalWhenDetected.
claims.quote: | When detected, require approval before joining | RequireApprovalWhenDetected | (default) Bots are detected and marked in the lobby. They're enforced to be in the lobby until explicitly admitted into the meeting. |

claims.where: controls[1].note; Why it matters; Governance guidance: Before rollout
claims.claim: The external-bots guide documents a Do not detect bots option alongside detection with approval.
claims.quote: | Do not detect bots | AllowBots | Bots aren't detected or marked in the lobby or in the meeting. They appear as any other external participant in the meetings. |

claims.claim: The Set-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy reference additionally documents BlockDetectedBots to block detected external bots.
claims.quote: BlockDetectedBots: When detected, external third-party meeting bots and meeting assistants are blocked from joining meetings hosted in the organization.

claims.claim: The existing control is in Teams admin center > Meetings > Meeting policies > policy > Meeting Join and Lobby > Manage external bots and their access to meetings.
claims.quote: This setting is present in the Meeting Join and Lobby section of Meeting policies. Look for "Manage external bots and their access to meetings" and select the appropriate option.

claims.claim: Set-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy -Identity <policy name> -ExternalBotAccessMode RequireApprovalWhenDetected configures the existing detection-and-approval policy.
claims.quote: RequireApprovalWhenDetected: When detected, bots will be enforced to the meeting lobby, regardless of the lobby setting of the meeting. They will require approval before getting access to the meetings. This is the default value.
claims.fix: Keep the call. Append to controls[1].note: 'The external-bots guide names Set-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy but its code examples use Set-CsTeamsEventsPolicy; the linked MicrosoftTeams cmdlet reference documents the meeting-policy call shown here.'

claims.claim: The Teams Bot Identification Program is a public preview for software vendors building meeting bots.

Microsoft Teams Bot Identification Program (Public Preview)
Microsoft is also introducing the Teams Bot Identification Program to support independent software vendors (ISVs) that build meeting bot experiences for Teams.

claims.claim: The Bot Identification Program lets eligible bot vendors register with Microsoft.
claims.quote:
Through this program, eligible bot providers can register with Microsoft and include a self-identification marker in their meeting join requests.
The public preview has reached its current bot provider capacity.
claims.fix: Add after the program description: 'The public preview has reached its current bot provider capacity; Microsoft says it will publish onboarding guidance and next steps when the program becomes generally available.'
